brightwater-transit.title: Brightwater Transit: live bus tracking
brightwater-transit.text: Brightwater Transit's 1,200 buses each send a GPS event every 10 seconds to an Azure event hub, which an eventstream reads. Each event holds BusId, RouteId, Speed, DelayMinutes and a raw Payload string. Events land in a RawGps table in an eventhouse. Planners want a parsed table, Positions, kept up to date as data arrives without a separate scheduled job, and Positions must never miss rows that reached RawGps. An in-house dispatch app reads events from the eventstream and must receive only events whose DelayMinutes is above 5. The dispatch board shows, every minute, each route's average speed over the last 5 minutes. Most queries cover the last 14 days, and data older than one year must be removed. Dispatch supervisors must run KQL queries on the eventhouse but must not change any table or the eventstream, and each must get a Teams message as soon as one of their buses runs more than 15 minutes late.

fernway-telemetry.title: Fernway Energy: a slow, noisy telemetry platform
fernway-telemetry.text: Fernway Energy streams readings from 20,000 smart meters through an eventstream into an eventhouse, and a nightly pipeline copies daily summaries into a lakehouse table that a Direct Lake semantic model reads. Engineers report that the lakehouse table now holds over 100,000 small files, the nightly pipeline copies 300 meter regions one at a time, and dashboards query the last 30 days of readings far more than anything older. Nobody is told when the nightly pipeline fails.

harbor-analytics.title: Harbor Health: setting up a governed analytics workspace
harbor-analytics.text: Harbor Health is moving its reporting to Fabric. The data team of six engineers will build in a Dev workspace, and finished work moves through Test to a Production workspace. Engineers must be able to create and edit items but not manage access. Fifty analysts only read reports and query curated tables with SQL. Patient email addresses must be hidden from analysts in query results, and every curated item that holds patient data must carry the organization's Confidential label.

larkspur-orders.title: Larkspur Outfitters: nightly order loads
larkspur-orders.text: Larkspur Outfitters runs its web shop on an Azure SQL database. Every night a Fabric pipeline loads the Orders table (about 400 million rows, a LastModified column set on every insert and update, about 1% of rows change each day) into a bronze lakehouse, and a notebook builds silver and gold Delta tables from it. When the source is slow the pipeline retries, and some nights the same batch of orders has landed twice. New customers are created in the CRM, which syncs to the lakehouse once a day, so orders sometimes arrive for customers the Customer dimension doesn't have yet.

marlow-sales.title: Marlow Grocers: a slow nightly warehouse load
marlow-sales.text: Marlow Grocers loads point-of-sale data into a Fabric warehouse, SalesDW. Every night each of its 600 stores exports a Parquet file of about 2 MB to Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2, and a pipeline loops over each file's rows and runs one INSERT statement per row into a staging table, which takes most of the night. A stored procedure then merges the day's rows into FactSales, which holds about 3 billion rows and has an IDENTITY key named SaleId, and updates DimStore; the two changes must succeed or fail together. FactSales was created without data clustering, and most report queries filter it on a range of SaleDate. A second pipeline that applies customer returns runs UPDATE statements against FactSales at the same time as the sales load, and one of the two often fails with an update conflict even though they never change the same rows. The returns load must run after the sales load, whether the sales load succeeds or fails.

quarry-hill-monitoring.title: Quarry Hill Labs: catching failures before the scientists do
quarry-hill-monitoring.text: Quarry Hill Labs runs its lab-results platform in one Fabric workspace. A nightly pipeline runs two Copy activities, CopyAssays and CopyBatches, that load instrument files into a lakehouse in about two hours, and then a notebook that cleans the results. Both Copy activities connect to a single Office 365 Outlook activity through On fail. Some instrument files hold rows whose values don't fit the destination's data types: the copy must keep going, and the team must be able to see which rows were left out. Several Dataflow Gen2 items in the workspace also refresh reference data. Workspace monitoring is turned on. The four-person operations team holds the Viewer role in the workspace, and it wants to query the monitoring logs with KQL and get a Teams message whenever a Dataflow Gen2 refresh in the workspace fails.

quillon-claims.title: Quillon Insurance: locking down a claims warehouse
quillon-claims.text: Quillon Insurance keeps its claims in a Fabric warehouse named ClaimsDW. Forty regional adjusters connect to it with SQL tools. They were given only the Read permission on the warehouse through item sharing, and the data team grants them table access with T-SQL. Each adjuster may see only the claims of their own region; a table named dbo.AdjusterRegion maps each adjuster's user name to a region. The dbo.Claims table has a FraudScore column that adjusters must never read. An external auditor with no workspace role needs read-only T-SQL access to every table in ClaimsDW for one quarter. Reports built on ClaimsDW carry the Highly Confidential label, and data that reviewers export from them for offline review must keep it. Policy details live in an Azure SQL Database used by the policy administration system, and analysts want them in Fabric in near real time without building or scheduling load pipelines.

tidewater-releases.title: Tidewater Freight: moving changes from Dev to Production
tidewater-releases.text: Tidewater Freight's shipping team works in three workspaces, Ship-Dev, Ship-Test and Ship-Prod, assigned to the Development, Test and Production stages of one deployment pipeline. Ship-Dev is connected to the main branch of an Azure DevOps repository. The five engineers hold the Contributor role in Ship-Dev, and each must build features without disturbing the others' work. The ShipDW warehouse is developed as an SDK-style SQL database project: a publish to development may drop columns, but a publish to production must stop if it would lose data. The ShipLake lakehouse has a shortcut to an Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 container of carrier files, and each stage must read its own container. A notebook, LoadShipments, must use each stage's own lakehouse. A semantic model built on ShipDW must refresh every morning in Production.
